en: *Ṣaṇmukhī-dhyāna-śikṣā-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Originally composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga and commented upon by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

Now, desiring to benefit all sentient beings by enabling them to practice both mundane and supramundane concentrations so that they may swiftly abandon all afflictions, I shall set forth these skillful means.
The verse says:
Those seeking liberation accumulate [merit]; dwelling therein, they practice with diligence.
Having attained the three perfections, these are persons who rely on the cultivation of meditative concentration.
The commentary states:
This first verse generally indicates six categories.
The term "those seeking liberation" refers to persons who seek liberation.
"Accumulation" refers to the ability to accumulate the provisions for sublime practice.
Regarding "diligently cultivating while abiding," causing the mind to dwell well upon its object of focus is called meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because it is undistracted and unwavering.
Question:
How is it cultivated?
It means that once the three perfections have been attained, one relies upon a person who practices meditative concentration.
There are three perfections: first, the perfection of teacher and disciple; second, the perfection of the object of focus; and third, the perfection of mental attention.

There are also three bases, namely these three concentrations: first, concentration with directed thought and sustained thought; second, concentration without directed thought and with only sustained thought; and third, concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought.
One who cultivates meditative concentration refers to one capable of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

If a person can give rise to a mind of aspiration for liberation, has further accumulated the provisions for liberation, relies upon meditative concentration, possesses the three supports such as a teacher and so forth, and practices with these supports, then through the cultivation of concentration, they will be able to attain worldly merits as well as excellent and perfect fruits.
Having first established the sequence in this manner, it is called the general heading.
The verse says:
Those who delight in liberation within the three vehicles are called persons seeking liberation.
When both types of obstacles are completely eliminated, this is called liberation.
One should know that the appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*) is the essential nature of these two obstacles;
because it contains the seeds of afflictions and all [karmic] seeds, it is able to bind the two kinds of persons.
The afflictive obscurations have already been eliminated, yet the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been removed;
this is called the Śrāvaka vehicle. The remainder can only be severed by a Buddha.
Even if those delusions are absent, their conduct appears as if they still possessed them.
"These habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have arisen previously; if they were removed, it would be different from this.
The commentary states:
These four verses explain the seeker of liberation, meaning that there are distinctions regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
To take delight in liberation within the context of the Three Vehicles is called "seeking liberation.
What is liberation?
The complete removal of the two kinds of hindrances is what is termed liberation.
What are these two obstacles, whose removal constitutes liberation?
One should know that the appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*) is the essential nature of the two obstacles; this "consciousness" is precisely the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
"Appropriation" (upādāna) has the meaning of "basis"; it refers to the essential nature of the two obstructions: the afflictive and the cognitive.
Furthermore, what are these?
The seeds of delusion are the very nature of the afflictive obstruction, while all seeds are the very nature of the cognitive obstruction.

Furthermore, "all seeds" refers to the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), which are capable of binding two types of persons: the seeds of the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) bind the *śrāvaka*, while the seeds of all [obstacles] bind the Bodhisattva, because they act as fetters for the *śrāvaka* and the Bodhisattva respectively.
What is the distinction between these two types of liberation?
It is said that while Śrāvakas have not yet eliminated their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they realize liberation by severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to eliminate them entirely.
What is habitual tendency (*vāsanā*)?
Although those afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer exist, the physical postures and behaviors they produce are as if they possessed those afflictions; this is called habitual tendency.

Here it should be said: if, although the afflictions are absent, they cause those [postures] to manifest as if they possessed afflictions—this statement that "the performed postures are as if they possessed afflictions" is because the name of the effect is applied to the cause.

Those referred to are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. They do not know that this is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of someone else; they think it is merely the residual impression of actions habitually performed in previous lives. Although their delusions have now been exhausted, the appearance of their conduct still resembles that of defiled behavior, and this is termed "habitual tendency."
If one can eliminate and sever that which is different from this, it should be said:
"If those habitual tendencies are all absent, one does not perform the ritual as one would for an affliction.
The verse says:
Planting all roots of goodness, Free from doubt and removing the fever of affliction,
Purified within the stream of the Dharma— This is called accumulation.
Able to uphold and delight in hearing the Dharma, Skillfully eliminating the two views.
"Yet hearing [the Dharma] alone brings joy and contentment; these four matters should be known.
The commentary states:
These two verses explain the meaning of "accumulation."

As it is said in the Sūtra: "This person should first cultivate extensive learning and listen to the true Dharma; having correctly eliminated the feverish afflictions of various views, they can correctly subdue the hindrances and entanglements of the mind."
Based on the meaning of this passage, the first verse is spoken.
How does one accumulate all roots of goodness?
It is by means of being able to uphold the True Dharma.
Taking this as the prerequisite, it causes wholesome qualities such as faith to increase.
What is meant by being free from doubt?
It refers to delighting in hearing the Dharma.
By virtue of knowing the Dharma, all doubts—both those already arisen and those yet to arise—are entirely extinguished.
How does one eliminate feverish affliction?
It means by eliminating the two views.
What are the two views?
First, the view that desires to be recognized by others; second, the view that gives rise to self-exaltation.
This refers to forming such a thought as follows:
"To cause others to know that I am a person of virtue" is called the view of causing others to recognize one's own qualities.
Based on this view, desiring to exalt oneself is called the view of self-exaltation (*ātmotkarṣadṛṣṭi*).
Because these two cause the mind to become parched and feverish, they are called "tormenting heat" (*paridāha*).
What is the purity of the flow of the Dharma?
It refers to being able to dispel the mental state of finding satisfaction merely upon hearing the Dharma.
The phrase "the removal [of obscurations] above" flows into this context.

Regarding "the purity of the stream of the Dharma": it means that when listening to the Dharma, the mind flows in a continuous succession without distraction; because the mind is pure, the hindrances and entanglements are stilled.
If one listens to the Dharma without weariness and can further advance in contemplation and diligent cultivation without ceasing, only then can it be called the purity of the stream of Dharma.
One should know that this refers to the stages of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, which should be understood in their respective order.
Next, there are sixteen verses explaining the application of diligence in abiding.
The first verse provides a general summary, while the remaining ones offer detailed explanations.
The verses state:
The object of focus and the essence, The distinctions and mental attention,
Distraction of mind, abiding, and the provisions, Cultivation of concentration, renunciation, and the fruit.
Regarding the "object of focus," there are three kinds.
External, superior, and internal—these three objects of focus give rise to [the mind];
one should know that there are three modes of abiding, wherein the essence of the mind remains undisturbed.
Commentary:
Regarding the three types: first, external conditions; second, superior conditions; and third, internal conditions.
External conditions refer to the images manifested through practices such as the contemplation of white bones; these constitute the sphere of the beginner.
The superior object refers to the signs of tranquility and so forth within the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.
The internal object refers to taking as an objective domain the sign manifested from mental verbalization (*manojalpa*).
Its own essence refers to the state of the mind being undisturbed, which is termed "abiding."
"One whose mind is undisturbed" means that when the three kinds of objects are present in external neutral spheres, the mind remains unmoved and undisturbed according to those objects.
The verse says:
Only one who abides in the primary application and possesses a concentrated mind can perceive it.
With no shifting of thought regarding objects, this continuity makes one a wise person.
In the second dwelling, one is endowed with appropriate practice;
with a mind weary of and detached from the world, tranquil and focused, with no shifting of thought, this continuity makes one a wise person.
In the third abiding, one should correspondingly remain fixed upon the object before them;
with a concentrated mind free from shifting thoughts, one who maintains this continuity is a person of clarity.
The commentary states:
These three verses correspond, in their respective order, to the external, the superior, and the internal.
Regarding the phrase "the mind does not shift toward objects," it means that the mind is not distracted by other objects; therefore, it is called "non-shifting."
"Continuity" means firmly maintaining the mind so that it is not interrupted.

One is called a "person of clarity" because, either through personal reflection or following the instruction of another, they apply themselves to the practice of the dharma of meditative concentration; such a person is termed a person of clarity.
It should be understood that these correspond, in order, to the lineages of those who follow the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) and those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
Regarding the phrase "with a mind of weary detachment, tranquil, single-minded, and without shifting mindfulness," this means that one generates a mind of weary detachment toward its objects.
Previously, one observed the object alone but was unable to give rise to revulsion; now, through focused concentration, the mind gives rise to revulsion and detachment without distraction.

Regarding "abiding steadily upon the former object": this means that when one takes as an object the phenomena manifested by mental discourse (*manojalpa*), the mind becomes concentrated and fixed upon that object. Therefore, it is said: "One whose mind is settled, whose thoughts do not shift, and whose mindfulness is continuous is a person of clarity."
The verse says:
Firm adherence and the correct flow, Along with concealing and examining its meaning,
Attaining joy of mind upon turning [the mind], And when the factors of the antidote arise.
Delusion arises and can be pacified; The preparatory application is constant and uninterrupted;
One is able to practice the path of spontaneity; It should be known that there are nine non-distractions.
Commentary:

Within those dwellings, there are nine distinctions: namely, the initial dwelling, the dwelling of right mindfulness, the dwelling of retrospective examination, the dwelling of subsequent distinction, the dwelling of pliancy, the dwelling of tranquility, the dwelling of subjugation, the dwelling of effortful application, and the dwelling of spontaneity.
All of these are practiced according to the sequence of the phrases in the Āgama sūtras.
When one first trains in taking an object as a focal point, the mind’s firm adherence to it is called the "initial abiding."
Subsequently, causing right mindfulness to flow continuously without interruption is called "abiding in right mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
If, relying upon this, a distracted mind arises and one further examines the object of focus while remaining established therein, it is called "abiding in re-examination" (*pratyavekṣaṇāsthiti*).
Next, at a later time, when a further distinction is attained, it is called the "subsequent distinct dwelling" (*paścād-viśeṣa-vihāra*).
Next, at a later time, when the antidote arises and the mind attains mastery, giving rise to joy, it is called the "pliant dwelling" (*praśrabdha-vihāra*).
When the antidote of non-attachment arises toward this craving and delight, and the mind becomes tranquil, being free from fondness and attachment, it is called "abiding in tranquility.
Subsequently, in order to subdue all afflictions—both those already arisen and those yet to arise—that constitute heavy obstacles, it is called "abiding in subduing."

Subsequently, at a later time, when the mind of application (*prayoga-citta*) dwells upon a single object of focus, following it continuously without interruption, this is called "dwelling with effort" (*abhyāsa-sthiti*).

Subsequently, at a later time, when the mind dwells upon the object of focus without application, flowing spontaneously and entering meditative absorption continuously through the path of familiarization, this is called "spontaneous dwelling" (*svarasa-sthiti*).
When these nine types of mind do not disperse, it is called "abiding.
One should understand that this term "non-dispersion" is to be applied in conjunction with "firm adherence" and so forth.
The verse says:
With exertion and with interval, With application and without application;
Among these, one, six, two, and four— One should know these as the modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
That is to say, external and internal adverse conditions, coarse heaviness, and mental application—
these five types of mental distraction are contrary to one who abides in meditative concentration. Among them,
the distraction of outward scattering refers to the lack of tranquility regarding the object upon which the mind is fixed.
One should know that mental agitation, depression, and attachment to flavors constitute internal distraction.
One should recognize the signs of improper objects of focus—namely, thoughts of one's kin and so forth—which give rise to two kinds of self-grasping;
this is called the distraction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
When one sees a preceding object clearly and discriminates its characteristics, this is the distraction of mental engagement (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*);
other than this, there is only the mind of mindfulness.
Within the distraction of mental engagement, there further arises the characteristic of that distraction.
Regarding the vehicles and meditative concentrations, the first two should be eliminated.
The commentary states:

One should know that there are four kinds of mental attention (*manasikāra*): first, mental attention of exerted bearing; second, mental attention of interrupted bearing; third, mental attention of effortful bearing; and fourth, mental attention of effortless bearing.
In this context, firm persistence without distraction is the mental attention of "strenuous bearing," because it involves bearing the burden through the initial application of effort.

Subsequently, the six types of non-distraction, such as "correct flow" and so forth, constitute the mental attention of "interrupted bearing," because during the intervals there is the frequent arising of distracted thoughts.
The preparatory application for the uninterrupted state is the mental attention of bearing the burden through effortful practice.
Entering the path of familiarization is the mental attention of bearing the burden through effortless practice.
Having thus summarized them as one, six, and two, it should be understood that these constitute the four types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Furthermore, there are five kinds of mental distraction:

first, external mental distraction; second, internal mental distraction; third, mental distraction due to improper objects; fourth, mental distraction due to coarseness and heaviness; and fifth, mental distraction due to mental attention.
External mental distraction occurs when, at the time of engaging with an object of focus, the mind subsequently flows out toward other matters.
Internal mental distraction refers to the three states, such as restlessness (*auddhatya*), which arise in a disordered manner amidst the objects of focus.
Distraction due to improper conditions refers to the arising of longing and attachment for relatives and acquaintances while practicing meditative concentration.
Distraction due to coarse mental states refers to the two forms of self-grasping that cause the mind to become disordered.
In the practice of meditative concentration, there are these two matters: namely, benefit and harm.
If the body is at ease and secure, it is called benefit; if the body is weak and frail, this is its harm.
Some say, "I now experience pleasure," or "I now have suffering.
Some say, "This is my pleasure," or "This is my suffering.
In this context, the term "I" (ātman) carries the sense of grasping or clinging.
Regarding what is called "mental distraction through attention," there are three types.
When one dwells with clear manifestation upon the signs of the object of focus, this is of the nature of investigative reflection (*vitarka*).

Alternatively, when one moves from this vehicle to another vehicle, or from this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to another absorption—specifically at the time of intense conceptualization and investigative reflection—one thereby causes the mind to become disturbed; this is termed mental distraction.
"Distinct from this, there is only the mind of mindfulness": this serves as the antidote to the distraction of initial mental attention (*manasikāra*).

By not engaging in conceptual discrimination while taking an object as its focus, there is merely the mind of mindfulness; this clarifies the accomplishment of the mind's non-forgetfulness of mindfulness.

Regarding these three types of distraction, the first two should be abandoned; however, the third is not a fault, as it involves proceeding from one meditative concentration to another out of a desire for excellence.
The verse says:
Abiding in ethical discipline, with ethical discipline purified, Is the dwelling place of the provisions.
One should know that the four bases of purity consist of: guarding the sense faculties and so forth;
practicing correctly regarding objects; supporting the basis [of practice];
and diligently cultivating wholesome deeds, which can eliminate all faults.
First, one attains attention (*manasikāra*); next, one attains worldly purity;
further increasing this, one dwells in the supramundane. These three concentrations bring about rebirth in the three realms.
Commentary:

Regarding those who abide in the provisions: this means that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the basis for boundless merit; one must first abide in ethical discipline, ensuring that its practice is pure and free from transgression.
If one seeks purity of precepts, there are four causes:

first, properly guarding the sense faculties; second, knowing the proper measure in eating and drinking; third, being able to maintain self-vigilance during the first and last watches of the night and remaining in accord with meditative concentration; and fourth, dwelling in right mindfulness amidst the four modes of deportment.
Why does one guard the sense faculties and so forth to purify ethical discipline?
Because when one practices correctly regarding objects and their basis, these support one another; by diligently cultivating wholesome qualities, one is able to eliminate faults.
First, the cause is the purity of conduct regarding the objects of engagement.
Second, it is the mutual support and conformity of the physical basis, through moderation in the consumption of food and drink.
Third, because one initiates diligent effort toward wholesome deeds;
fourth, because one is able to eliminate faults by applying the mind skillfully to conduct and deportment.
Through these four causes, ethical discipline attains purity.
It should be understood in this way: through three types of concentration, one attains three kinds of renunciation.

When taking external objects as the focal point, one attains abiding in mental attention; when taking superior objects as the focal point, one attains mundane purity; and when taking the internal mind as the focal point, one attains supramundane purity.
One who abides has attained permanent deliverance; they will certainly proceed toward nirvāṇa and never regress.
Having thus explained the diligent cultivation of abiding, the verse says:
One who is learned and has seen the truth, who speaks well with compassion,
and always gives rise to a joyful mind— such a person is fit to be taught concentration.
They exhaust all matters as they are and speak according to how things truly are.
One who well understands the objects of knowledge is called a teacher of the Dharma.
From hearing, one gives rise to mental engagement; this is said to be the cause of cessation.
This mental engagement with the cause of cessation is what is called "well-perfected."
The commentary states:
There are three kinds of perfection: first, the perfection of teacher and disciple; second, the perfection of the object of focus; and third, the perfection of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Herein, the first verse describes the perfection of teacher and disciple, which signifies that such a person possesses perfection in skillful instruction, perfection in realization, perfection in eloquent speech, perfection in an untainted mind, and perfection in the application of continuous teaching.
This demonstrates that the teacher possesses the perfection of all virtues; through such a teacher, one hears the true Dharma and attains realization.

Next, the second verse is taught to clarify the perfection of the object of focus (*ālambana*): teaching things exactly as they are, in their full extent, regarding the objects to be well-known is called "well-spoken" (*svākhyāta*).
This clarifies that because the teacher and disciple can expound all matters exhaustively and without stinginess, it is called the "perfection of the object of focus" (*ālambana-paripūri*).

Next, the third verse is taught to clarify the "perfection of mental attention" (*manasikāra-paripūri*); this demonstrates that since the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) arising with hearing as its cause serves as the direct cause for the Noble Path and Nirvana, all mental attentions directed toward this mental verbalization attain perfection.
In this context, the word "cause" (*hetu*) indicates hearing, which is the cause for mental verbalization (*manojalpa*).

That which is called "quiescence" (*śānta*) refers to both *nirvāṇa* and the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), because they are quiescent by their very nature and are capable of leading toward quiescence.
In summary, regarding "mental attention to the cause of tranquility" (*śamatha-hetu-manasikāra*): this clarifies that this mental attention takes the cause of cessation as its object.
What is meant by the "object"?

It is the realization that phenomena lack intrinsic nature; when one attends in this way, that very act is both the cause and the cessation itself. Therefore, this mental attention is called "the cause of tranquility"—this is an etymological explanation based on identity (*ekārtha-vyākhyā*).
Furthermore, this attention (*manasikāra*) based upon that is also called the "cause of tranquility" (*śamatha-hetu*); this is the explanation of the specific phrase. The verse states:
According to this explanation, it should be said "attention that is the cause of tranquility. The traditional rendering as "appropriate attention" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is not a literal translation.
That is to say, it refers to the mental verbalization of seeking; following this, one should engage in detailed investigation.
When mental discourse ceases, that is concentration;
being without other objects and without signs, the mind abides by taking syllables as its object.
This is the state of mental tranquility, which is called *śamatha*.
Observing those various objects is called vipaśyanā;
it is also a single yoga, termed the "one-and-two-part concentration. One should know that there are two kinds of concentration:
that which removes the obstacle of coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) and that which removes the obstacle to vision (darśana-āvaraṇa).
It can serve as the antidote to this, acting as a skillful means for cultivating long-term goodness.
The commentary states:

Next, it clarifies that those who practice meditative concentration based on a support must necessarily have a basis of reliance; that is, seeking and so forth are explained in relation to the three concentrations.
The term "seeking" (vitarka) indicates that there is initial inquiry;
since it is stated that there is initial inquiry, one may infer by analogy that there is also sustained investigation (vicāra).
The term "subtle examination" indicates the state of being without initial inquiry and possessing only sustained investigation.
The statement that "mental discourse is absent" is intended to reveal the absence of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
Since both vitarka and vicāra have mental discourse as their essential nature, this definition is established according to the dharma of śamatha (calm abiding).
The statement regarding "no other object" (*ananyālambana*) and so forth clarifies the meaning of non-differentiation.

When the mind abides by taking only those syllables as its object, it is called "no other object" and is also termed "signless" (*animitta*), because the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the characteristics of the meaning within that contemplation does not possess those [external] signs.
This dwelling is called *śamatha*. *Śama* has the meaning of "calming" or "stopping," while *tha* has the meaning of "place.
It is not that *śamatha* alone exhausts all activities. Rather, it refers to the place where the mind comes to rest;

the mind attains a state of concentrated stability by relying on meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This absorption is precisely the place where the mind is concentrated and dwells, and is therefore named *śamatha*; apart from this, it does not exist.

Next, based on the method of *vipaśyanā*, its definition is clarified by the following single verse: "That which relies upon multiple objects is called 'contemplation of the multitude' (*vicitra-bhāvanā*).
As for the word "that" (*tat*), it refers to that which is connected with both [the preceding factors], namely *śamatha* and the term "object of focus" (*ālambana*).
This is because one attains *vipaśyanā* by relying on *śamatha*, as various contemplations arise based on all meanings contained within the locus of the syllables (*akṣara*).

Within the state of tranquility (*śamatha*), all meanings rely upon the syllables; that is to say, the observation arising in dependence upon these various meanings is called "contemplation of the manifold" (*anupaśyanā*).

Regarding what is called "the concentration with one or two parts": sometimes there is only the state of tranquility (*śamatha*) without the various modes of observation (*vipaśyanā*); sometimes there are the various modes of observation but not the state of tranquility; and sometimes both are present. One should know that this is precisely the union of tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-yuganaddha*).

Furthermore, there are two kinds of obstacles to śamatha and vipaśyanā, namely the obstacle of coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) and the obstacle of views (dṛṣṭi). It should be understood that the two meditative concentrations are their respective remedies, to be applied in their proper order.
Why are these two called the "expedient means for increasing the wholesome"?
Because they are the expedient means that can increase wholesome dharmas.
How does one cause these expedient dharmas to attain complete purity?
The verse says:
This purity should be known as consisting in the cultivation of three aspects:
tranquility, exertion, and equanimity; these should be understood according to their respective order.
If the mind sinks and fears submergence, arouse conditions for sublime objects;
if agitation arises and fears excitation, cultivate disenchantment to cause its cessation.
Free from sinking and agitation, let the mind abide in equanimity.
Flowing effortlessly without striving, one constantly cultivates the three characteristics.
The meditator cultivates these three characteristics; they do not cultivate just one in isolation.
This is to prevent faults such as mental sinking and to further purify the mind.
The commentary states:
To answer the preceding question, those who seek pure concentration cultivate three types of characteristics.
What are these three?
These are tranquility (śamatha), exertion (pragraha), and equanimity (upekṣā).
Furthermore, how are they cultivated?
They should be understood according to their respective order.
Whenever their afflictive obscurations arise, one should practice the subsequent stages of cultivation accordingly.
At what time should this be done?
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of these practices?
Furthermore, regarding the application of the modes of exertion (*pragraha-nimitta*) and the signs of elevation (*abhyunnata-nimitta*):
if the mind is sunken or fears sinking into meditative absorption, one should cultivate the three signs as will be explained below.
If the mind is sunken, one may cultivate the mode of exertion and the sign of elevation.
What is this? It has the characteristic of causing the mind to rejoice by taking a sublime object as its condition.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristic of calm abiding (*śamatha*): if the mind is agitated or if there is a fear of agitation, one should cultivate the state of tranquility.
What is this? It is the cultivation of revulsion so as to bring about their cessation.
One generates intense aversion toward the objects of focus and causes the transgressions within one's own internal mind to subside.
The characteristic of equanimity refers to being free from dullness and agitation.
In what state of mind does this occur?
It occurs when the mind abides in equanimity.
This characteristic of equanimity is precisely the effortless, spontaneous flow of constantly cultivating the three characteristics.
When one cultivates these three characteristics in this sequential order, those who practice concentration attain the characteristic of purity.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that śamatha and so forth are themselves concentration (*samādhi*), one does not cultivate only one of these three characteristics.
Why? Because it is for the purpose of preventing faults such as mental sinking (*laya*).
Furthermore, to purify the mind: if one practices only *śamatha* (calm abiding) and the internal mind becomes sunken, then when it is sunken, one should exert effort to uplift it.
If the mind becomes agitated and distracted due to such exertion, one should contemplate the object of impurity (*aśubha*) to give rise to renunciation.
When one correctly cultivates this sign of equanimity, it is called right concentration capable of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*); by means of this, the mind is rendered utterly pure.
One should understand that all of this accords with the phrases of the authentic sūtras and should be contemplated in accordance with reason.
The verse says:
Renunciation and joyful aspiration, Abiding correctly and possessing capability—
When these obstructing afflictions are all removed, The mind of the one in meditative concentration is purified.
The commentary states:
This explains the benefit of purification according to the *Dharmapada-sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a person desires to seek purity of the inner mind, yet is confronted by the manifestation of delusive obstacles that they cannot eliminate, and wishes to sever them, they should first refrain from committing great transgressions regarding the paths of unwholesome karma; they should cease sinful views and seek to go forth into homelessness, aspiring for liberation."

If, while dwelling in the middle [state], afflictions such as desire, hatred, and malice arise, giving rise to unwholesome discursive thoughts that obstruct superior delight (*prīti*), one speaks of "delight" to indicate the removal of this obstruction.
If subtle discursive thoughts regarding kin, worldly matters, or immortality obstruct one’s right abiding (*samyak-sthiti*), one speaks of "right abiding" as the remedy for these.
If one must apply effort (*ābhoga*) in order to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this concentration lacks the nature of functional capacity (*karmanyatā*).
If one can eliminate [this effort], it manifests as having the capacity to remove afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, the term "functional capacity" is used.
This demonstrates that one who possesses pure concentration attains four kinds of superior benefits.
What are the fruits for one who cultivates concentration?
The verse says:
Within this gateway of meditative concentration, the correct cultivation described therein brings all mundane concentrations to clear understanding,
and one also comes to know supramundane concentration.
The meaning of this verse is to show that those who cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* obtain manifest results.

If a person can practice according to the described characteristics of meditative concentration, they will attain the perfection of the supreme fruits of all worldly realms as well as supramundane fruits, as previously explained.
Question: As explained above, what matter does this seek to clarify? Answer:
Revealing the basis for the underlying intention, The fundamental basis and the actual basis,
The perfection of worldly meditative concentration, And the understanding of that which transcends the world.
Commentary:
This verse is spoken to provide a concise explanation that encompasses the full meaning, in order to harmonize with what was previously stated.
As it was said at the outset:
"The seeker of liberation" indicates the perfection of intention (*āśaya*), while "the one who has accumulated" indicates the perfection of the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This clarifies that one who possesses the mind and cultivates meditative concentration must necessarily rely upon the accumulation of provisions (*sambhāra*).
The phrase "one who diligently practices while abiding" reveals the perfection of the fundamental basis.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "You should first rely on meditative concentration to be able to exhaust all outflows; this is what I have taught."
"If one wishes to seek liberation from the ocean of birth and death, there is no other expedient means than right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

The phrase "attaining the three perfections" reveals the perfection of the right basis, clarifying that the teacher and disciple have received the transmission such that it may be definitively relied upon.
Regarding those who rely on the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this demonstrates the perfection of practice.

When wise persons, as previously described, remain free from negligence and engage in correct cultivation, all mundane concentrations become fully perfected, and they are able to realize all supramundane states; this demonstrates the perfection of the attainment of the fruit.
*Ṣaṇmukhī-dhyāna-śikṣā-śāstra*, one fascicle.
